speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The social glue has come unstuck and we are forced online to learn, work, live and stay connected.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet there are many who are cut off from access due to lack of internet connectivity, requisite devices or digital literacy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They are not digital natives; they are digital outcasts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: COVID-19 has exposed and deepened the digital divide in our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve an SGUnited Smart Nation, closing this gnawing digital divide must be an urgent priority.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that Deputy Prime Minister acknowledged this divide in the Fortitude Budget earlier.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In this Motion, I will address three questions: how deep is the digital divide?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty-one percent have a computer, a personal computer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Contrast this with 96% and 95% respectively of households living in non-HDB apartments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These numbers mean that some of us are almost guaranteed to have internet connectivity and a personal computer, while more than five in 10 households living in 1- and 2-room HDB flats have no internet access or personal computer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is also reflected in the ground realities exposed by Home-based Learning (HBL).

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A few community groups I personally know including Engineering Good have given out more than 2,600 laptops in total.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They have also provided wi-fi dongles or SIM cards to several families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The bleak picture does not end at infrastructure, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Stories from the ground reveal significant struggle in terms of digital literacy and skills, particularly among one, low-income households; two, the differently-abled; and three, seniors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: ReadAble is a community organisation supporting families in rental flat communities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They shared that parents struggle with navigating donated laptops donated – whether with Zoom or even in-app functions, which compromises their children’s education.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: According to Society Staples, a social enterprise working with the differently-abled (PWDs) and the Disabled Persons Association, many lower income PWDs lack equipment, Internet access or the necesssary IT skills.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is difficult for them to work from home or participate in society online.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This can mean loss of income and opportunities to retrain or learn new skills.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They also missed out on maintaining or even expanding connections with family and friends which increases mental stress and strains existing coping mechanisms, especially for those with psychosocial disabilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Cassia Resettlement Team, a community organisation, has had to support many low-income individuals, particularly seniors, who struggle with the digitisation of Government services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, many of them cannot use SingPass without help.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: SingPass, as we know, is required to access many such services including checking CPF accounts, which are regularly required to apply for welfare schemes; or checking medical appointments, medical tests results and prescriptions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In 2006, the Intelligent Nation or iN2015 Masterplan pledged that every household with a school-going child would own a personal computer by 2015.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I remember this clearly as I was running my own education technology company then and was very energised by this vision of a digital future which my company also participated in.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly, despite this iN2015 ambition, our efforts to become a Smart Nation since 2014 and the Digital Readiness Blueprint released in 2018, we continue to struggle with a deep digital divide in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Market forces are the key driver of this divide.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Today, Internet connectivity and personal computers are necessities but they are still priced beyond the reach of the low-income in our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While it has benefited more than 40,000 households, the scheme falls short in several ways.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, it only permitted one laptop per eligible household regardless of the household size, increasing to two only last month due to HBL.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the application process is complex and bureaucratic.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Third, it is limited in scope, excluding pre-school, home-schooled and university students and adults.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, it discriminates against PWDs, who only receive a 50% subsidy as compared to 75% for students.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, under the Home Access Scheme, adults have no option to apply for a personal computer, only a tablet or smartphone.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: MOE worked with schools to loan out personal learning devices and kept schools open for those who struggled with digital access.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The device loan programme came with conditions and liability provisions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Community organisation 6th Sense shared that there were families who were too scared to bring these devices home as they would not be able to afford to pay the schools if the devices got lost or broken.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Further, the families were rightly worried about going to school and risk COVID-19 infection.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One teenage student I know developed severe COVID-19 related-anxiety before HBL.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Why should any child be required to go to school and use IT facilities at the height of a pandemic?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given these gaps, community organisations found that it made more sense to give every family good internet connection and every child a personal computer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: By personal computer, I mean a laptop or a desktop, and not a tablet.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Personal computers, including laptops, are the engines of creativity and productivity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Tablets and smartphones are not enough for work and learning.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A child who has to type out an essay on a smartphone or a tablet is not on the same footing as a child with a laptop.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, some low-income families reported that their children were told to do home-based learning on their mobile phones!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I commend the policy intent, but I propose a broader, cross-Ministry change in the form of a Digital Adequacy Framework on which I will elaborate later.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Now, let me move to the gaps in our statistical metrics and KPIs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They do not capture whether every citizen has internet access commensurate with their needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As they influence and inform policy-making, it is important to get them right.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, our statistics do not reflect the sufficiency of devices in each household.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, they measure the number of houseFholds with access to a personal computer, which includes tablets.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if a household of seven has one tablet to share between them, they are classified as having access to a personal computer in the home.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Simply owning a personal computer and being connected to wi-i is not the end of the matter.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Poor connection or an underperforming hardware creates further obstacles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Xiaoqian, a Secondary 2 student, recently shared her home-based learning experience on a public podcast.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Before ReadAble provided her with a new laptop, she only had an old laptop at home.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I quote from her: “It will be very slow for me to switch on and I have to wait.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I wake up early to switch on the computer to wait for it, but in the end I was late for class because it was still uploading.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I wouldn’t have a full lesson.” I am sure we will agree that it is unacceptable in a Smart Nation for a child to receive a deficient education because of faulty hardware.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Third, our KPIs conflate personal computers with other digital devices.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is undesirable for reasons I have already discussed earlier.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If our metrics do not highlight these fault lines, we remain blissfully misinformed of reality and true digital inclusion will continue to elude us.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I support this commitment, Mr Deputy Speaker, and would like to offer some suggestions from the ground regarding enhancements to existing schemes and structural changes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The NEU PC Plus Scheme could be further streamlined.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The five gaps I mentioned earlier should be plugged.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, beneficiaries of various financial assistance schemes could automatically qualify for new PC Plus.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, can MSF and MOE work together to ensure that every family with a child on MOE-FAS, or every family supported by ComCare who has a child in school, automatically gains adequate access to a fully subsidised personal computer?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Should adults supported under ComCare or residing in HDB rental flats not have the option of receiving a partially or fully subsidised digital device, depending on their income.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: IT subsidy schemes should also include device replacement and customer care.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The scheme should also be broadened immediately to permit applications to benefit all children whether pre-school, home-schooled or university students, and adults from low-income families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: PWDs should be subsidised equally to students, especially given the changing nature of work post COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The vouchers could be stipulated for use only with local SMEs which would also directly assist our local enterprises in these trying times.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of a structural rethink to realise the Digital Readiness commitment to provide adequate digital access for those with limited resources, I propose that a Digital Adequacy Framework be considered.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because it is not enough to just be digitally ready or included, this digital participation must adequately support their learning, work and social connections meaningfully.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Under this Framework, tablets must be decoupled from the definition of “personal computer” across the board for learning and work purposes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We should also view the amount of hardware deemed adequate for each household to be the aggregate of the needs of each member in it.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, should every student aged Primary 5 and above have their own laptop, considering MOE’s digital literacy plans for upper Primary schools?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Should younger children have computer access in the home, sharing a personal computer with no more than one other person?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Framework should also fold Internet speed, hardware functionality and digital literacy into its analysis to enable meaningful digital participation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can IMDA and HDB work with commercial providers and Town Councils to ensure that all low-income households have adequate Internet connection?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, can Wireless@SG be expanded to cover all rental flats in Singapore and enhanced with sufficient speed, much like the ubiquitous wi-fi access available in shopping malls?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Much public policy has been characterised by efficiency, effectiveness and economy, emphasising outcome that are easily measured rather than what might be most helpful to measure.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such information will be helpful to policy design.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our clarion call for SGUnited must surely be a Singapore that is also digitally united through community digital resilience.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that Deputy Prime Minister also acknowledged this need for resilience through digital inclusion earlier in his speech.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The observations and recommendations outlined in this speech have been the result of consultative and collaborative efforts with, and between, these community groups and citizens.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am energised by this vision, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: COVID-19 has thrust Singapore into the digital future.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must not leave any citizen in the past.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun, would you like to join the debate?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In her speech, she has vividly captured the wide range of ground difficulties encountered by families on the wrong side of the digital divide.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As Leo Tolstoy posited in his renowned novel Anna Karenina: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." Indeed, families in Singapore that have struggled with digital access over the circuit breaker period juggling home-based learning and work from home have faced a spectrum of challenges.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Some have had no devices, others the wrong kinds of devices, of which many were slow or malfunctioning.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And yet others had no Internet connections and still more had limited digital skills.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Families on the right side of the digital divide are similarly happy – robust Internet connections, reliable devices, and digital competencies to see them through their online needs for learning, working and transacting.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: How can we level the playing field as far as such technological needs are concerned?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As far back as nine years ago, in 2011, the United Nations declared Internet access as a human right.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With Industry 4.0 pounding at our doors, regarding digital access as a public utility makes eminent sense and will involve three tranches.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The first is to make Internet connection universal.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's Wireless@SG programme already provides free Internet access across broad swathes of public space.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, our transition towards 5G provides a strategic opportunity to "reset" our digital infrastructure networks for universal Internet access.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The second tranche is ensuring access to computing devices.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As those of us who own multiple devices well know, they are not all created equal and some devices are simply more effective for particular functions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As it stands, online learning platforms are optimised for computers or laptops, and not mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot expect our students from low-income households to simply get by or make do with mobile phones for online learning.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Possible channels include building computing provision as part of school registration, ComCare benefits, or WIS.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Stepped levels of subsidies according to household income and size of household could also be introduced, similar to the subsidy ladders for childcare and Baby Bonuses.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Technology companies should be mobilised to co-fund such provisions as part of their corporate social responsibility efforts.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The final tranche is of course digital literacy.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Invariably, better-educated parents will be more tech-savvy and can better guide their children's digital access.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hitherto, some donors have been reluctant to provide Internet access to needy families, citing fears that they will be vulnerable to online risks such as pornography or gambling.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We must therefore introduce more intensive in-school digital literacy programmes to help these children make up for the lack of scaffolding at home.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But poor digital literacy should not be used as justification to deny low-income families access to a vital resource that the rest of society benefits from.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond learning for children, home-based computing will also be essential if low-income adults are to have any real chance to participate in more technology-based training or employment.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The progress of our Smart Nation drive has translated into more Government services moving online, thus making digital access even more of a need than a want.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In a rapidly digitalising society, comprehensive digital access in the form of wi-fi, devices and technological literacy is a critical social leveller as a conduit for education, upskilling and employment.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: The recent slew of generous budgetary measures shows that our Government is committed to leaving no one behind.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our Digital Readiness Blueprint, which was launched in 2018, envisions a nation with universal digital access where every Singaporean – young or old, disabled or able, rich or poor – is empowered with access and skills to thrive in the digital future.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: While our digitalisation message has been consistent and universal, the adoption of digital technologies has been uneven, across our economy and across our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: COVID-19 has brought that same message across more starkly, highlighting to all the value and even the urgency of digital solutions at a time when we have all had to learn and work from home, and interact and transact online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We now have the opportunity to give digitalisation a renewed impetus and push and the Nominated Members of Parliament have already observed that the Deputy Prime Minister has been somewhat prescient in his Fortitude Budget speech by making digital inclusion one of the key thrusts of the Fortitude Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But I think I want to make one point before I go further, which is, I appreciate the spirit in which some of the ideas have been put forward, but in our efforts to highlight gaps and in our desire to do better, we must be careful not to forget the progress that has been made, largely because of the hard work done by various Government officials in partnership with community partners and corporate partners.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, I want to begin by first putting into perspective the current state of Singapore's digital readiness.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Where are we today in our digital inclusion journey?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: If we exclude tablets from the definition, we find that 61% of households with school-going children own computers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Interestingly, within this group, it is noteworthy that more than 80% of HDB 1- to 3-room households with school-going children have access to computers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, it is gratifying that the efforts are reaching this lower income group.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: IMDA's survey also indicates that broadband penetration among households stood at 98% in 2019; and it is nearly universal for households with school-going children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Another group that we pay close attention to is our seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Smart phone usage among adults below 60 was 99.6% in 2019; for seniors aged 60 and above, it had increased to 75% from 36% in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These figures, I believe, affirm that we have made valuable progress in our digital inclusion journey.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: One key contributory factor has been the range of initiatives that have been launched in close collaboration between our public, private and people sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And I want to assure Ms Ong that the computers in this scheme refers to computers as in PCs and desktops and not tablets.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: A further 16,500 households have benefited from IMDA's Home Access programme since 2014 which provides subsidised Internet access, with an option to bundle in an Internet-enabled device.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Both these are run in partnership with self-help groups and also with Social Service Agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Digital readiness is also not just about hardware and connectivity, but it is also about the literacy and the skills to derive the full benefit.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And that is why we have, for example, initiatives like the Silver Infocomm Initiative (SII), which was launched as far back as in 2007.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It provides a range of programmes for seniors at different levels of digital skills.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These programmes are also provided in vernacular languages to meet the needs of our seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our companies have been important partners in these initiatives, with over 70 partnering IMDA, with 6,000 volunteers in our outreach efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And for persons with disabilities, the NEU PC Plus programme provides support for computer and broadband access.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I can elaborate further but because of the time constraint, I just want to emphasise that the persons with disabilities remain an important part of our overall effort towards digital inclusion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, we have a range of programmes aimed at youths, aimed at seniors, aimed at people with disabilities, aimed at low-income households, and these programmes are run in partnership with the private sector, with the community organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The situation, I believe and I beg to differ with the Member, is not as bleak as Nominated Member of Parliament Anthea Ong paints it out to be.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I think we have made progress, but at the same time we must have the humility to acknowledge that there is more that we can do.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And that brings me to the impact of the COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It has led to a surge in the interest and demand to go digital.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We welcome this rejuvenated interest and will do our best to support it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The question has been asked, "Why only one device per household in the NEU PC programme?" But we are talking about an environment pre COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I think that Members would agree that the last two months has changed the world.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, what was sufficient in a pre COVID-19 era for example – one computer per household at a time when there was no home-based learning, there was no work-from-home or telecommuting requirements – changes dramatically when you are in a COVID-19 type situation with circuit breaker measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, I think we must have some perspective in evaluating how fit-for-purpose the programmes were and of course, then understand that if the situation has changed, we need to adapt and introduce the measures that are necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, I think it has been an important effort.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have also seen commendable initiative spawned by self-organised groups and community organisations.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.
